key_insight: Latent-flow world models can train stably, but still lose the ability to move manipulated objects because the supervision is too sparse to teach when motion should happen. The paper shows the issue is not the latent representation itself, but the training signal—and that adding decode-based rollout supervision can restore meaningful motion.
problem_solved: This paper addresses the failure of latent world models to preserve controllable motion during manipulation tasks. Specifically, it explains why pretrained flows become nearly static, and why retraining with latent-only losses often produces unnatural, teleport-like changes instead of smooth movement.
method: Diagnose the root cause of motion collapse in latent-flow world models by analyzing the training supervision.
Show that anchor-sparse, latent-only losses do not specify where along the rollout horizon changes should occur.
Restore motion by augmenting training with decode-based rollout supervision that ties latent predictions back to observable frame-level dynamics.
impact: This work helps practitioners build world models that remain cheap and stable without sacrificing motion fidelity. It is especially relevant for robotics, simulation, and video prediction systems where accurate object dynamics are essential for control and manipulation.

paper_title: Frozen Flows Forget: Diagnosing and Restoring Lost Motion in a Latent-flow World Model
paper_authors: Xiwen Chen, Rigaudiere Z. Li, Zhiruo Zhou, Xiaojun Zhu, Houde Liu
